chart.burden.callout: 26.5% of renters pay half or more of income in 2024

provenance.population: every metropolitan area with renters in the census tables, 2005 to 2024 (392 metros in 2024)

chart.burden.sql:
select year,
       sum(renters_burdened) / sum(renters_with_share) as burdened_share,
       sum(renters_severe) / sum(renters_with_share) as severe_share,
       sum(owners_mortgage_burdened) / sum(owners_mortgage_with_share) as owner_mortgage_burdened_share,
       sum(case when median_rent_share < 0.30 then 1 else 0 end) as metros_median_under_30,
       count(*) as metros
from mart_metro_year
where kind = 'metropolitan' and renters_with_share > 0
group by year
order by year
chart.burden.subtitle: Renter households by the share of income their rent takes, nationally by year, with the thirty and fifty percent lines
chart.burden.title: The median renter is burdened in 51% of metros in 2024, so the median hides nothing; the problem is the whole distribution, with 26.5% of renters paying half or more (interval 25.7% to 27.2%). The national series moved and stayed moved in 2009, 2015, 2021.

provenance.population: every purchase loan on a principal residence in the extract, 2018 to 2025 (2,722,577 loans from 4,341 lenders in 2025)

chart.buyers.sql:
select year,
       sum(loans) as purchase_loans,
       sum(under_35) * 1.0 / sum(loans) as under_35_share,
       sum(over_2x) * 1.0 / sum(loans) as over_2x_share
from mart_borrowers_income
group by year
order by year
chart.buyers.subtitle: Purchase borrower income over the local median, and the share of buyers under 35, by year, with lender bootstrap intervals
chart.buyers.title: The buyer is richer than in 2019 by +0.15 of the local median income (interval +0.12 to +0.19) and, against the claim, slightly younger: the under 35 share rose +1.2 pts (interval +0.1 pts to +2.3 pts) by 2025. The ratio moved most in Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim +0.44; Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach +0.37; New York-Newark-Jersey City +0.30.

chart.decision.callout: median breakeven 10.0 years; the median household can afford the median home in 221 of 382 metros

provenance.population: every metropolitan area with an anchored value, a census income and rent in 2024 (382 metros; 382 with enough history for the breakeven)

chart.decision.sql:
select cbsa_code, cbsa_title, year, rate, value_anchored, median_income, renter_median_income, median_rent, payment_share
from mart_metro_year
where kind = 'metropolitan' and year = (select max(year) from mart_metro_year where median_income is not null)
  and value_anchored is not null and median_income is not null and median_rent is not null
order by payment_share desc
chart.decision.subtitle: Renter wealth less owner equity by horizon for the largest metro at 6.72%, with the breakeven marked and its interval across metros
chart.decision.title: Buying beats renting only after 10.0 years in the typical metro (interval 1.0 years to beyond 30 years), and one point of rate moves the breakeven by +4.5 years. Longest to break even among the largest metros: Boston-Cambridge-Newton 21 years; Chicago-Naperville-Elgin 20 years; San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont 18 years.

chart.definition.callout: 283 of 375 metros sit above their 2006 payment share in 2024

provenance.population: every metropolitan area with a census income and an anchored value, 2005 to 2024

chart.definition.sql:
select year,
       sum(value_anchored * owner_households) / sum(owner_households) as median_home,
       sum(price_to_income * owner_households) / sum(owner_households) as price_to_income,
       sum(payment_share * owner_households) / sum(owner_households) as payment_share
from mart_metro_year
where kind = 'metropolitan' and payment_share is not null and owner_households > 0
group by year
order by year
chart.definition.subtitle: Price to income and the payment share of income on the median home, owner weighted across metros, 2005 to 2024
chart.definition.title: The payment share of 2024 does not exceed 2023; the payment story is not yet the largest the window has seen. It sits +1.1 pts above 2006 (interval +1.0 pts to +1.3 pts), so the 2006 peak is passed, and the window's own peak is 2023.

chart.migration.callout: placebo -0.78% against headline +1.48% per person per hundred

provenance.population: 385 metropolitan areas with migration over 2020 and 2021 and the index in both windows (85 states)

chart.migration.sql:
with migration as (
    select cbsa_code,
           100.0 * sum(case when year in (2020, 2021) then domestic_migration end) / avg(case when year in (2020, 2021) then population end)
           - 100.0 * sum(case when year in (2018, 2019) then domestic_migration end) / avg(case when year in (2018, 2019) then population end) as migration_shock,
           100.0 * sum(case when year in (2018, 2019) then domestic_migration end) / avg(case when year in (2018, 2019) then population end) as migration_pre,
           100.0 * sum(case when year in (2017, 2018) then domestic_migration end) / avg(case when year in (2017, 2018) then population end) as migration_placebo_level
    from mart_metro_year where year in (2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021) group by cbsa_code
),
growth as (
    select a.cbsa_code,
           ln(b.index_nsa) - ln(a.index_nsa) as growth,
           ln(d.index_nsa) - ln(c.index_nsa) as placebo_growth
    from mart_metro_quarter a
    join mart_metro_quarter b on b.cbsa_code = a.cbsa_code and b.period = '2021Q4'
    join mart_metro_quarter c on c.cbsa_code = a.cbsa_code and c.period = '2016Q4'
    join mart_metro_quarter d on d.cbsa_code = a.cbsa_code and d.period = '2018Q4'
    where a.period = '2019Q4'
)
select m.cbsa_code, d.cbsa_title, d.states, m.migration_shock, m.migration_pre, m.migration_placebo_level, g.growth, g.placebo_growth, p.population
from migration m
join growth g using (cbsa_code)
join (select cbsa_code, cbsa_title, states, population from mart_metro_year where year = 2021 and kind = 'metropolitan') d using (cbsa_code)
join (select cbsa_code, population from mart_metro_year where year = 2021) p using (cbsa_code)
order by m.migration_shock desc
chart.migration.subtitle: Price growth 2019Q4 to 2021Q4 against the migration shock per hundred residents (over 2020 and 2021 less 2018 and 2019), with the placebo window beside it
chart.migration.title: The metros that gained people were already lagging before the pandemic: the placebo on the years before it is -0.8% (interval -1.4% to -0.2%), so the headline of +1.5% price growth over the window per person gained per hundred residents beyond the pre pandemic pace is a lower bound on what the migration itself did.

chart.ranking.callout: 17 of 20 move beyond their rank interval; rank correlation 0.94

provenance.population: every metropolitan area present in both the index and the census release of 2024 (382 metros); micropolitan areas excluded

chart.ranking.sql:
select cbsa_code, cbsa_title, households, value_anchored, median_income, payment_share,
       rank() over (order by value_anchored desc) as raw_rank,
       rank() over (order by payment_share desc) as adjusted_rank
from mart_metro_year
where kind = 'metropolitan' and year = (select max(year) from mart_metro_year where median_income is not null)
  and value_anchored is not null and median_income is not null
order by adjusted_rank
chart.ranking.subtitle: The 20 largest metros ranked by the price of the median home and by the payment share of local income, 2024
chart.ranking.title: The ranking changes when you hold constant what people earn there: 17 of the 20 largest metros move beyond their intervals. Less affordable than their price says: Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater from 106 to 90; Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach from 33 to 22; Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim from 7 to 2. More affordable: St. Louis from 223 to 307; Minneapolis-St. Paul-Bloomington from 114 to 195; Washington-Arlington-Alexandria from 25 to 102.

chart.rate_shock.callout: rate part +$549 against price part +$839 in 2026Q2

provenance.population: every metropolitan area with quarterly prices from 2019Q1 and loans in the base and test years (388 metros, 86 states)

chart.rate_shock.sql:
with base as (
    select cbsa_code, payment as base_payment, value_anchored as base_value, rate as base_rate
    from mart_metro_quarter where period = '2019Q1'
)
select q.period,
       sum(q.payment * w.owner_households) / sum(w.owner_households) as payment,
       sum(b.base_payment * w.owner_households) / sum(w.owner_households) as base_payment
from mart_metro_quarter q
join base b using (cbsa_code)
join (select cbsa_code, owner_households from mart_metro_year where year = 2019) w using (cbsa_code)
where q.year >= 2019 and q.kind = 'metropolitan'
group by q.period
order by q.period
chart.rate_shock.subtitle: The monthly payment on the median home from 2019Q1: the part from the price and the part from the rate
chart.rate_shock.title: The rate part of the payment overtook the price part in 2023Q3. The rate shock froze turnover where owners had the most to lose: 0.06 fewer purchases per 100 owner households per point of lock in (interval -0.08 to -0.03), and the placebo on the years before the shock sits at 0.00 with an interval that includes zero.

chart.rate_shock.lock_in.callout: Change in purchase originations per 100 owner households, 2023 onward against 2018 and 2019, by originations under four percent per 100 owners

provenance.population: every metropolitan area with quarterly prices from 2019Q1 and loans in the base and test years (388 metros, 86 states)

chart.rate_shock.lock_in.sql:
with intensity as (
    select cbsa_code,
           100.0 * sum(low_rate_originations) / max(case when year = 2021 then owner_households end) as lock_in_per_100
    from mart_metro_year where year between 2019 and 2021 group by cbsa_code
)
select m.cbsa_code, m.cbsa_title, m.year, m.turnover_per_100_owners, i.lock_in_per_100, m.owner_households, m.states
from mart_metro_year m join intensity i using (cbsa_code)
where m.kind = 'metropolitan' and (m.year in (2018, 2019) or m.year >= 2023) and m.purchase_loans is not null
order by m.cbsa_code, m.year
chart.rate_shock.lock_in.subtitle: Change in purchase originations per 100 owner households, 2023 onward against 2018 and 2019, by originations under four percent per 100 owners
chart.rate_shock.lock_in.title: Turnover fell by 0.06 purchases per 100 owners per point of lock in; placebo 0.00

chart.supply.callout: a metro at the 90th percentile of building (2.55 per 100) against the 10th: -17.7% over 5 years

provenance.population: 385 metropolitan areas over 5 windows of 5 years (1925 cells, 85 states)

chart.supply.sql:
with annual as (
    select cbsa_code, cbsa_title, states, year, index_at, households, population, permits, domestic_migration,
           100.0 * permits / households as permits_per_100_households,
           100.0 * domestic_migration / population as migration_per_100
    from mart_metro_year where kind = 'metropolitan'
),
windows as (
    select cbsa_code, cbsa_title, states,
           floor((year - 2001) / 5) as window_id, min(year) as first_year, max(year) as last_year,
           avg(permits_per_100_households) as permits_rate, avg(migration_per_100) as migration_rate,
           max(population) as population
    from annual where year >= 2001 group by cbsa_code, cbsa_title, states, floor((year - 2001) / 5)
)
select w.*, (ln(e.index_at) - ln(s.index_at)) / (w.last_year - w.first_year + 1) as annual_growth
from windows w
join annual e on e.cbsa_code = w.cbsa_code and e.year = w.last_year + 1
join annual s on s.cbsa_code = w.cbsa_code and s.year = w.first_year
order by w.cbsa_code, w.window_id
chart.supply.subtitle: Annual price growth against the building rate the year before, 5 year windows, with the fitted slope under both specifications
chart.supply.title: Where builders kept pace, prices rose less: 8.0% less price growth over 5 years per extra permit per hundred households (interval -14.3% to -1.7%); without the demand control the estimate is -0.4%.

ch8.pushback.value: A payment is not the whole cost of owning: the cost model adds taxes, insurance, maintenance and the costs of buying and selling, but not the roof that fails in year four, and it credits the renter with a return the renter has to earn. The paths are drawn from the metro's own past, which includes a decade nobody expects to repeat, and the interval is the spread of those paths, not a forecast. The down payment years assume a renter who saves a tenth of income with no help and no return, which is the simplest honest reading of the question.
